Learned borrowing from Latin austrum. Distant cognate to leste.
Borrowed from Latin austrum (“south”).

parole.significato: Austrian (of, from or relating to Austria)

Semi-learned borrowing from Latin absentia (“absence”).

parole.significato: author (originator or creator of a work)

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese abtor, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin actor, from āctus + -tor. Doublet of ator.
Learned borrowing from Latin auctōritātem.
Learned borrowing from Latin autographum. By surface analysis, auto- + -grafo.
Learned borrowing from Latin auxiliāris.
Learned borrowing from Latin auxilium.

parole.significato: greed, avarice (excessive or inordinate desire of gain)
parole.testo: From Latin avāritia; possibly a semi-learned term. Doublet of avarícia.
From Latin avārus.

parole.significato: avarice (excessive or inordinate desire of gain)

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese avelãa, from Latin abellana (“filbert, hazelnut”). Cognate with Galician abelá, Spanish avellana, Occitan avelana and Romanian alună.

parole.significato: adventurer (someone who goes on an adventure)
parole.testo: From aventura (“adventure”) + -eiro (“-er”), from Old Galician-Portuguese aventura, from Latin adventūra, feminine of adventūrus (“about to arrive”), from adveniō (“to arrive”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese aviinça, a semi-leaned borrowing from Latin advenientia (“arriving”). Cognate with Galician avinza and Spanish avenencia.
Ultimately from Latin vērificāre. Doublet of verificar.
Borrowed from Latin āversiōnem.

parole.significato: the inside of an item of clothing
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin āversus.

parole.significato: to make agree; to bring into agreement; to appease
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin advenīre. Doublet of advir.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin advīsāre, from ad + vīsō; cf. also Spanish avisar, English advise, French aviser.

parole.significato: used for the fractions (or equal parts) of a unit divided in more than 10 equal parts; -th
parole.testo: From the ending of oitavo (“eighth”), from Latin octavus (< Proto-Italic *oktāwos), from octo (“eight”), possibly suffixed with Proto-Indo-European *-wós. Sense 2 is a back-formation from centavo (“cent”, literally “one hundredth”), from cento /cem (“one hundred”) + avo (“-th”).

parole.significato: to task; to give a responsibility (to)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin advocāre. Doublet of advogar and avogar.

parole.significato: to advocate (to express or encourage support for)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin advocāre. Doublet of advogar and avocar.
From Old Galician-Portuguese avondar, from Latin abundāre (“to overflow; to abound”). Doublet of abundar.

Learned borrowing from Latin axiōma, from Ancient Greek ἀξίωμα (axíōma).

parole.significato: sour; acid; sharp; tangy (of a taste)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese azedo, from Latin acētum (“vinegar”).
From Latin acidiva. Cognate with Galician acía.
Inherited from Latin aegyptiācus [diēs] (“fateful day”, literally “Egyptian day”), alluding to the Plagues of Egypt. Doublet of egipcíaco. Compare Spanish aciago.

parole.significato: goshawk (bird of prey in the genus Accipiter)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese açor, from Latin accipiter (“hawk”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese auçon, from Latin āctiōnem.

From Latin ad (“to, toward, at”) + ibī (“there”). Compare Galician aí, Spanish ahí.
Borrowed from Latin Babylōnius, from Babylōn (“Babylon”).

parole.significato: bacillus (any bacteria in the genus Bacillus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bacillum.
From vade-mécum, from Latin vāde mēcum (literally “go with me!”).

parole.significato: berry (soft fruit which develops from a single ovary and contains seeds not encased in pits)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin bāca (“berry; fruit”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bainha, from Latin vāgīna (“sheath”). Compare Galician vaíña, Spanish vaina, Catalan beina, also French gaine, Italian guaina. Doublet of vagem and vagina and related to baunilha.
From Latin baiulāre (“to carry a burden”) or perhaps from Arabic بَجُلَ (bajula, “to be worshipped”).

parole.significato: to baa; to bleat (of sheep: to make its characteristic cry)
parole.testo: From Latin bālāre.
Borrowed from Latin balbūtīre, from balbus. Compare French balbutier.
Learned borrowing from Latin Baleāris.

parole.significato: whale (any of several species of large sea mammals of the order Cetacea, excluding smaller ones)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese balẽa, from Latin ballaena, variant of bālaena, from Ancient Greek φάλαινα (phálaina), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“to inflate, blow, swell”), from *bʰel- (“to bloom”).
Learned borrowing from Latin ballista, from Ancient Greek βαλλίστρα (ballístra), from βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”). Doublet of besta.
From Latin balneāris.
Learned borrowing from Latin balneārius.

parole.significato: bowline (a rope to which a knot is tied to lift volumes or to support the man working on the side of the ship, on masts…
parole.testo: From Latin balteus. Doublet of bálteo.

parole.significato: bathtub (a large container for holding water in which a person may bathe)
parole.testo: From banho + -eira, from Latin balneum (“bath”).
Inherited from Latin blatta.

Inherited from Latin barbātus.
From Latin barbarismus.
Learned borrowing from Latin barbaricus, from Ancient Greek βαρβαρικός (barbarikós, “foreign, strange”).

parole.significato: barbarity (something barbaric or the act of being barbaric)

Borrowed from Latin bardus, from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *bardos.

Borrowed from (Medieval) Latin basilica, from Ancient Greek βασιλική (basilikḗ, “royal”), from βασιλεύς (basileús, “king”).

parole.significato: to beat; to beat up (to attack someone violently)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bater, from Latin battere, from earlier battuere. Compare Galician bater.
From abatina, from Latin abbatīna.
From Latin baptista, from Ancient Greek βαπτιστής (baptistḗs).
Learned borrowing from Latin bdellium.

parole.significato: someone who has been beatified by the Catholic Church

From beber + -dor, or from Latin bibitōrem.

Possibly from Latin via + -eco, cf. Italian vico.
From Old Galician-Portuguese beijar, from Latin bāsiāre.

parole.significato: purslane (a plant of the family Portulacaceae, especially Portulaca oleracea)

Semi-learned borrowing from Latin benedīcere. By surface analysis, bem + dizer. Doublet of benzer.

parole.significato: blessing (divine or supernatural aid or reward)
parole.testo: From bendizer + -ção, corresponding to Latin benedictiōnem (probably a semi-learned adaptation; compare the inherited doublet bênção).

parole.significato: Benedictine (of or pertaining to the Order of Saint Benedict)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Benedictīnus. By surface analysis, Benedito + -ino.
Borrowed from Latin beneficiārius (“enjoying a favor, granted a privilege”) from beneficium (“benefit”).
Borrowed from Latin beneficentia.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese beneficio, borrowed from Latin beneficium.

parole.significato: contributor (a benefactor; someone who gives to charity or some cause)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bene meritus.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bẽeizer, from Latin benedīcere. Doublet of bendizer. Compare Galician beicer.

parole.significato: beneficial (helpful or good to something or someone)

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese besta, probably borrowed from Latin bēstia (“beast”). Doublet of bicha.

parole.significato: crossbow (weapon consisting of a bow mounted on a stock)

Borrowed from Latin beta, from Ancient Greek βῆτα (bêta). The slang sense is a semantic loan from English beta.

parole.significato: mouth (the opening of a creature through which food is ingested)

parole.significato: a small, cheap and possibly insalubrious tavern
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Latin apothēca, from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē, “storehouse”). Doublet of adega, apoteca, botica, and butique.

parole.significato: box (any of various evergreen shrubs or trees)

parole.significato: balsam (sweet-smelling oil or resin derived from some plants)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin balsamum, from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (bálsamon).

Learned borrowing from Latin bellicus.

parole.significato: birch (any of various trees of the genus Betula)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin betulla, diminutive of Gaulish betua, from Proto-Celtic *betwiyos, *betuyā (“birch”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷet-. Compare Italian betulla, Spanish abedul, Catalan bedoll, French bouleau.

parole.significato: drunk; under the influence of alcohol

From Old Galician-Portuguese cabeça, from Vulgar Latin capitia, from the neuter plural (reanalyzed as a feminine singular) of Latin capitium, from caput.

parole.significato: cacophony (a mix of discordant sounds, potentially creating ambiguities)

parole.significato: each, every (qualifying a singular noun, indicating all examples of the thing so named seen as individual or separate i…

parole.significato: sternpost (timber or bar at the stern of a vessel)

From encruzilhar (“to cross”), from cruz (“cross”), from Old Galician-Portuguese cruz, from Latin crux (“cross”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, to bend”).

From Latin indūrēscere, from indūrō. By surface analysis, en- + duro (“hard”) + -ecer. Compare Spanish endurecer.

parole.significato: enema (injection of fluid into the rectum)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin enema, from Ancient Greek ἔνεμα (énema, “injection”), from ἐνίημι (eníēmi, “to send in, inject”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese enfermo, from Latin īnfirmus (“sick, feeble”), from in- + firmus (“firm”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer-mo-s (“holding”).

parole.significato: to thread (to put thread through an orifice, especially a pinhole)
parole.testo: From en- + fio (“thread”) + -ar, from Old Galician-Portuguese fio, from Latin fīlum (“thread”).

parole.significato: after a long time; eventually; at last

parole.significato: emphyteusis (long-term right to use a property on condition of taking care of it and paying taxes)

parole.significato: cove (a small coastal inlet, especially one having high cliffs protecting vessels from prevailing winds)

parole.significato: to deafen (to make deaf, permanently or temporarily)
parole.testo: From en- + surdo (“deaf”) + -ecer, or from Latin surdēscere, from surdus (“deaf”) + -ēscō. Compare Spanish ensordecer.

parole.significato: stepchild (the child of one's spouse and his or her previous partner)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese entẽado, from Latin ante nātus (“born before”).

parole.significato: to understand, to grasp, to comprehend
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese entender, from Latin intendere. Doublet of intender, a borrowing.

parole.significato: enthymeme (syllogism in which a premise or conclusion is implied)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin enthȳmēma, from Ancient Greek ἐνθύμημα (enthúmēma).

parole.significato: bowel (an internal organ of the stomach)

parole.significato: among (denotes a mingling or intermixing with distinct or separable objects)

parole.significato: to deliver (to transport something to a destination)

parole.significato: isthmus (narrow strip of land connecting two larger landmasses)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin isthmus, from Ancient Greek ῐ̓σθμός (ĭsthmós, “neck”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese isto, from Latin istud, neuter of iste (“that”).
Learned borrowing from Latin item (“also; in the same manner”).

Borrowed from Latin iaspis, from Ancient Greek ἴασπις (íaspis).

parole.significato: jet (impetuous outflow of a liquid or gas)

parole.significato: acre, a notional unit of area equal to the land that could be worked by two oxen or 50 men in one day
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin diāria opera (“daily work”). Compare Galician xeira and Asturian xera.

parole.significato: fasting (period of time when one abstains from food)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese jajũu, from Latin iēiūnium (“fast”), from iēiūnus (“hungry, abstinent”), from Proto-Italic *jagjūnos, itself from Proto-Indo-European *Hyeh₂ǵ-yu-, adjectival form of *Hyeh₂ǵ-ye/o- (“to sacrifice”). Compare Galician xaxún, xexún, French jeûne and Spanish ayuno. Doublet of

parole.significato: jejunum (central of the three divisions of the small intestine)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin jejunum, ieiunum. Doublet of the inherited jejum.

parole.significato: Used to express surprise, excitement or exasperation.
parole.testo: Relatinised from Old Galician-Portuguese Jesu, from Latin Iēsūs, from Ancient Greek Ἰησοῦς (Iēsoûs), from Hebrew ישוע (yeshúa).
Borrowed from Latin iocōsus.
From jogar (“to throw; to hurl”) + -dor, from Latin iaciō (“to throw; to hurl”).

parole.significato: to play (to participate in a sport or game)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese jogar, from Latin iocārī. Compare Galician xogar, Asturian xugar, Spanish jugar.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese jogo, from Latin iocus. Compare Galician xogo and Spanish juego.
Inherited from Latin diurna, from diēs (“day”).
Inherited from Latin diurnālis, from diēs (“day”).

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter J/j.

Perhaps from Latin clupea. Compare Galician xouba.

Learned borrowing from Latin iuba (“mane”).

parole.significato: to jubilate; to rejoice (to be very cheerful)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin iūbilāre.
Borrowed from Latin jubilaeus. By surface analysis, júbilo + -eu.

parole.significato: Jewish, Judaic (of or relating to (a) Jew(s))
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin iūdaicus, from Hebrew יהודה (y'huda, “Judah”).

parole.significato: Jew, Jewish person (adherent of Judaism or member or descendant of the Jewish people)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese judeu (“Jew”), from Latin iūdaeus (“Jew; Judaean”), from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), from Hebrew יהודי (Yehudi). By surface analysis, Judeia + -eu. Displaced the collateral form judio.
Borrowed from Latin iūdiciālis.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese judio, from Latin iūdaeus. Displaced by the more Latinate collateral form judeu.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese jugo, from Latin jugum, iugum, from Proto-Italic *jugom, from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm. The preservation of the -u- was likely due to metaphony.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese juiz, from Latin iūdicem. Compare Galician xuíz.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese jullo, julio, from Latin iulius.

Learned borrowing from Latin iuncus.

parole.significato: joint (part of the body where two bones join)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese junta, from Latin iūncta, from iūnctus, perfect passive participle of iūngō (“to join”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese juntar, from junto (“joined, together”), from Latin iūnctus (“joined”), present passive participle of iungō, from Proto-Indo-European *yewg-.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese junto, from Latin iūnctus, perfect passive participle of iungō, from Proto-Italic *jungō, from Proto-Indo-European *yunégti, from *yewg- + *-né-.
Borrowed from Latin iūnctiōnem.

parole.significato: juniper (shrub or tree of the genus Juniperus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin iūniperus, jūniperus. Compare the inherited doublet zimbro.

Inherited from Latin iūrātus. Cognate with Catalan jurat, French juré, Galician xurado, Italian giurato, and Spanish jurado, among others. Compare English jurat, derived from the same root (via Medieval Latin).
From Old Galician-Portuguese jurar, from Latin jūrāre, iūrāre (“to swear”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-.

From Old Galician-Portuguese jur, from Latin jūre, iūre, ablative of iūs, with inflection later altered in Portuguese, as if a derivative of the verb jurar; compare Spanish jur.

parole.significato: juridical, legal, judicial (pertaining to the law or rule of law)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin iūridicus.
Calque of Latin iūsta causa.

parole.significato: to juxtapose (to place side by side)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin iūxtāpōnō.

From Old Galician-Portuguese justiça, borrowed from Latin iūstitia (“justice”). Cognate with Galician xustiza, Spanish justicia, Catalan justícia, Occitan justícia, French justice, Italian giustizia, Sicilian justizzia and Romanian justiție. See also justeza, possibly a doublet.

parole.significato: free from sin and guilt; righteous
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese justo, from Latin iūstus (“just, righteous”), jūstus, from Proto-Italic *jowestos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-.
Borrowed from Latin iuvenīlis, derived from iuvenis (“young”). By surface analysis, joven (“young”) + -il (“-ile”).

parole.significato: youth (quality or state of being young)
parole.testo: Probably a semi-learned term taken from Latin iuventūtem (“youth”), from iuvenis (“young”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁en-.
Probably a semi-learned term taken from Latin jūdicium, iūdicium. Compare Spanish juicio.

parole.significato: already (indicating that something has happened before)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ja, from Latin iam (“already”). Compare Spanish ya.
Learned borrowing from Latin iūnior (“younger”), a contracted form of iuvenior (“younger”), from iuvenis (“young”). Influenced by English junior.

parole.significato: labyrinth, maze (complicated irregular network of passages or paths)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin labyrinthus, from Ancient Greek λαβύρινθος (labúrinthos).
Borrowed from Latin labōrem.
Borrowed from Latin labōrātōrem. By surface analysis, laborar + -dor. Doublet of lavrador and labrador.
Borrowed from Latin labōriōsus.

parole.significato: labrose (having thick lips; said of either edge of the aperture of a univalve shell)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin labrosus. By surface analysis, labro + -oso.
Learned borrowing from Latin lacerātiōnem. By surface analysis, lacerar + -ção.

parole.significato: lachrymose; tearful (having tears on one’s eyes; about to cry)

parole.significato: lacustrine, of or relating to a lake

parole.significato: laconic (using as few words as possible)
parole.testo: From Latin Lacōnicus (“Spartan”), from Ancient Greek Λακωνικός (Lakōnikós, “Laconian”).

parole.significato: litany (prayers recited by a leader alternated with responses from the congregation)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ledaỹa, from Latin litanīa, from Ancient Greek λιτανεία (litaneía, “prayer”). Cognate with Galician ladaíña. Doublet of litania.

parole.significato: pure (not influenced by cants and other languages)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin Latīnus (“Latin”). Doublet of latino (“latin”) and ladino (“sly”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese lado, from Latin lātus. Compare Spanish lado and Italian lato.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lagõa, from Latin lacūna (“pit”), from lacus (“lake; basin”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lókus (“lake, pool”). Doublet of lacuna and laguna.

parole.significato: layman (someone who is not an ordained cleric)

parole.significato: lambdacism (substituting an L for an R)

Inherited from Latin lambere (“lick, lap”).
Borrowed from Latin lamela.

parole.significato: to lament; to bewail; to feel sorry for
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lāmentāre.

parole.significato: to open slashes in [something] by hitting it with a cutting tool, such as for curing it

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lanterna, from Latin lanterna (“lantern; lamp”), corruption of Ancient Greek λαμπτήρ (lamptḗr, “torch”).

Learned borrowing from Latin lapidārius.
Borrowed from Latin lāpsus (“a sliding, falling”).

parole.significato: home (place or building where one dwells)

From Latin larix.

parole.significato: larva (early growth stage of some insects and amphibians)

parole.significato: Latin (of or relating to the Latin language)

parole.significato: Laurente (someone from the ancient Roman city of Laurentum)
parole.testo: From Latin Laurentius (“Laurente”), from Laurentum (“ancient city in Latium”).

From lavar + -dor, or from Latin lavātōrem. Compare Spanish lavador, Italian lavatore, French laveur.

parole.testo: Alteration of lavadoiro, from Latin lavātōrium, thus a doublet of lavatório. By surface analysis, lavar + -douro. Compare Galician lavadoiro.

parole.significato: layman (someone who is not an ordained cleric)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese leigo, from Latin lāicus (“lay; unconsecrated”), from Ancient Greek λαϊκός (laïkós, “of the people”), from λαός (laós, “the people”). Doublet of laico.

parole.significato: milkman (man who delivers milk early in the morning)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Latin lactārius, corresponding to leite + -eiro.
From Old Galician-Portuguese leito, from Latin lectus, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ-. Cognate of Spanish lecho, Italian letto and French lit.

parole.significato: milky (resembling milk in color or consistency)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese leitoso, from Latin lactōsus. By surface analysis, leite (“milk”) + -oso (“-ous”).

parole.significato: cat's ear (Hypochaeris radicata); smooth cat's ear (Hypochaeris glabra)

parole.significato: common name for various mosses within the genus Sphagnum

Inherited from Latin lignātōrem (“woodcutter; firewood collector”). By surface analysis, lenhar (“to chop firewood”) + -dor.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lenho, from Latin lignum.

From Old Galician-Portuguese lenço, from Latin linteum (“linen cloth”), from linteus, ultimately a probable borrowing from an unidentifiable source.
From Latin linteolum, from linteum, nominal form of linteus (“linen”), from linum (“linen; flax”).

parole.significato: leonine (relating or similar to a lion)

parole.significato: leprosy (infectious disease caused by infection by Mycobacterium leprae)

Borrowed from Latin leprōsus.

parole.significato: to read (to look at and interpret written information)

From Latin laetificus, from laetus (“cheerful, joyous”) + -ficus (“making”). Compare Italian letifico.
From Latin lētum (“violent death, ruin”) + -ficus.

From Old Galician-Portuguese leve, from Latin levis, from Proto-Italic *leɣʷis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ- (“light”). Doublet of léu.
From Old Galician-Portuguese leon (“lion”), from Latin leōnem (“lion”), from Ancient Greek λέων (léōn). Doublet of leu. Cognate with Galician and Spanish león among others.

parole.significato: indirect object of eles and elas
parole.testo: From Latin illis, dative plural of ille. Compare Galician lles, Spanish les.

Learned borrowing from Latin licentiāre.

parole.significato: market; marketplace (open area in a town housing a public market)
